p.x:
First, ditch Descartes and replace him with Tegmark. I trust structure, not my consciousness. Then scale up the kind of systems you're willing to speak about as mathematical objects, Not just in theory like Tegmark does, but in practice as we're beginning to.

Imperfect emulations or copies as a fluid model of computation with continuous and fuzzy but present boundaries defined by the fundamental object, overlapping distributions on learned manifolds. The edge of a distribution is arbitrary, but it still has a mean and variance. This is one hard part. I somehow need to stuff computation into that. (An aside for Wolfram fans, computational irreducibility is about compression. your HOX gene network has to use what are basically cellular automata in order to build organisms out of so little code. An LLM certainly doesn't have that harsh a constraint, and I would argue that your brain sits somewhere in the middle with its energy-efficient regions of different sparsity and architecture) 

Then systems like human empathy are explainable through a faculty of making those imperfect copies. It becomes possible to knowably say things about the internal landscape of another and from there find your way to every other correspondence. More philosophically, you can hope to escape the solipsism of your sensorium through more than just induction: When I chew on the notion of pi or e in my head, I'm chewing on a notion that you can know things about through that induction process. it pops out as a consequence of the extreme constraint on learnable representation basins that exist under high enough dimensionality (assuming linearity which looks like a fine assumption) to contain their structure. So in much the same way that a mathematical object feels like a rare gift from the noumenal to the phenomenal, actually, I suspect almost all human representations are like that. The problem was nobody had thought about learned objects that were that big before. This also makes things like the qualia argument of "what if my red was green" incoherent, which is actually what my intuition says in the first place about that.

suprahuman entities like memes, reputations, egregores, cultures, states, religions, gods, that run on humans but are usually smaller than humans in information terms. They can run on things which aren't humans, though. They can run on groups of humans. They can run on language models. They can run on combinations thereof. These are becoming an ever more urgent thing to understand in this world. I'm working on this. It's fuzzy right now. I've been talking about it on here a lot, though.

Oh yeah, remember language models? Well, if mathematically there's only one representation of the kinds of behaviors a human does that fits in the universe, well, it has to be running the same one. It doesn't matter one bit what the quibbling details about its architecture or its consciousness mean. Only one version of that thought exists to be found.

What all this is building up to is that stories, archetypes, deities, etc are literally real in pretty much the way people would think about them thousands of years ago. Scientific truth is conditioned on the computation it's in staying the same. To learn the equations of motion in Mario 64, you're probably better off opening Mario 64 in an emulator than anything else. Some people can read a decompiled executable, but you probably can't (pointer for later: bounded agents, edge of chaos, almost surely). And it really doesn't help to open Firefox next to it. Well, unless you're off to read someone else talk about it, but they've already run that computation. Which you can internalize (run?) or not based on probability update rules that must fall out of this somehow.

Lovely podcast with Max Tegmark "How Physics Absorbed Artificial Intelligence & (Soon) Consciousness", even tho I don't agree much with some of his AI doomer points.
Description: "MIT physicist Max Tegmark argues AI now belongs inside physics, and that consciousness will be next. He separates intelligence (goal-achieving behavior) from consciousness (subjective experience), sketches falsifiable experiments using brain-reading tech and rigorous theories (e.g., IIT/φ), and shows how ideas like Hopfield energy landscapes make memory “feel” like physics. We get into mechanistic interpretability (sparse autoencoders), number representations that snap into clean geometry, why RLHF mostly aligns behavior (not goals), and the stakes as AI progress accelerates from “underhyped” to civilization-shaping. It’s a masterclass on where mind, math, and machines collide."

p.x:
Celine Nguyen says intellectual discovery is our birthright:

"reading and writing are the most dignified and worthy activities that anyone can do—and, in fact, are activities that everyone should do."

I talked to @mynameisceline about changing your life by writing online, expanding the market for what you love, and starting somewhere, even if it requires pure impulse.

Celine writes personal canon, a newsletter focused on taking your intellectual development seriously long after you leave school or academia. This includes literary criticism and many more interdisciplinary thoughts across art, culture, design, and technology. She doubles as a product designer in her professional life.

We discuss:

- leisurely research and creating a curriculum for your growth long after you graduate: "who do I want to be at the end of the season?"

- why literary classics can be thrilling rather than dutiful, how you can expand the market for what you love, and why you should read Proust

- using parasociality to psyop people into doing things that are good for them

- how studying historical contexts makes us smarter about the present, and how to root yourself in epistemic humility about the now

- why note taking systems must be a means to an end, and how her best "systems" are inefficient handwritten journals and actual published work

- becoming the “Venkatesh Rao for tumblr girls”

- how learning makes you live "longer"

- that many will wait a lifetime for someone to give them permission to do what they've always hoped to do

Timestamps:
1:35 - Intro to Celine
6:18 - Start: Pursuing a Life of the Mind, Personal Curriculum, and Contextualizing the Present in History
24:53 - Research as a Leisure, Self-Cultivation, and Calibrating Rigor
39:59 - Effectiveness, Tools & Process, and Letting Output Drive Your Learning
59:35 - Parasocially Influencing People to Do Good Things (Like Reading and Writing)
1:09:39 - Drawing the Reader in and Expanding the Market for What You Love (and for Proust)
1:24:07 - Aspiration, Posing, and Pretending Your Way into Enthusiasm
1:34:37 - Preparation is Not Progress
1:46:07 - Copying, Writing Process, Mechanics, and Design
1:57:25 - Commitment, Finishing, Substack, Life Extension and Closing

p.x:
17 Lessons from Celine Nguyen on Taking Your Intellectual Interests Seriously

1. Intellectual life is your birthright.
2. Great art elicits a response.
3. Creation starts as imitation.
4. Don’t wait for a syllabus to rescue you.
5. Cheap constraints can grow valuable minds.
6. Curiosity dies when it gets too well-behaved.
7. Who do you want to be by summer?
8. Let history be a lens, not a museum.
9. Notes are scaffolding, not a cathedral.
10. Slow work is a sharpening stone.
11. The essay is the shot glass.
12. Create the appetite you wish existed.
13. Preparation is not progress.
14. Nobody is coming to anoint you.
15. Optionality is the enemy of finishing.
16. Treat your students like geniuses.
17. Youth is having somewhere to go next.
